content: Midazolam is a medication commonly used for sedation prior to diagnostic and therapeutic medical procedures. It belongs to the imidazole benzodiazepine class and exerts depressant effects on the central nervous system (CNS). The drug is characterized by its rapid onset of action and relatively minimal adverse effects. Midazolam can be administered through various routes, including oral, intravenous, intranasal, and intramuscular. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of midazolam as a sedative when administered before medical procedures. The evidence was gathered from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing midazolam to placebo or other sedative and analgesic medications. The review included studies involving participants of all ages, with midazolam administered at any dose or time prior to procedures, excluding dental procedures. A total of 30 trials involving 2,319 participants were included in the analysis. These trials assessed midazolam's use in various procedures, such as gastrointestinal endoscopy (16 trials), bronchoscopy (3 trials), diagnostic imaging (5 trials), cardioversion (1 trial), minor plastic surgery (1 trial), lumbar puncture (1 trial), suturing (2 trials), and Kirschner wire removal (1 trial). Comparisons were made between midazolam and other agents, including intravenous diazepam (14 trials), placebo (5 trials), etomidate (1 trial), fentanyl (1 trial), flunitrazepam (1 trial), and propofol (1 trial). Oral midazolam was compared to chloral hydrate (4 trials), diazepam (2 trials), diazepam combined with clonidine (1 trial), ketamine (1 trial), and placebo (3 trials). Intranasal midazolam was compared to placebo in 2 trials. The review identified a high risk of bias in 75% of the included trials due to inadequate reporting of randomization methods. Additionally, the effect estimates were imprecise because of small sample sizes. None of the trials reported allergic or anaphylactoid reactions. Intravenous Midazolam vs. Diazepam (14 trials, 1,069 participants): There was no significant difference in anxiety levels (risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 1.62; 175 participants, 2 trials) or discomfort/pain (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.49; 415 participants, 5 trials; I² = 67%). However, midazolam was associated with greater anterograde amnesia (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.66; 587 participants, 9 trials; low-quality evidence). Intravenous Midazolam vs. Placebo (5 trials, 493 participants): One trial reported that fewer participants receiving midazolam experienced anxiety (3/47 vs. 15/35; low-quality evidence). Another trial found no significant difference in discomfort or pain (3/85 in the midazolam group vs. 4/82 in the placebo group; P = 0.876; very low-quality evidence). Oral Midazolam vs. Chloral Hydrate (4 trials, 268 participants): Midazolam was associated with a higher risk of incomplete procedures (RR 4.01, 95% CI 1.92 to 8.40; moderate-quality evidence). Oral Midazolam vs. Placebo (3 trials, 176 participants): In one trial with 99 participants, midazolam significantly reduced pain (mean score: midazolam 2.56 [SD 0.49] vs. placebo 4.62 [SD 1.49]; P < 0.005) and anxiety (mean score: midazolam 1.52 [SD 0.3] vs. placebo 3.97 [SD 0.44]; P < 0.0001). However, two other trials did not find significant differences in anxiety scores. For example, one trial reported a mean anxiety score of 1.7 (SD 2.4) for midazolam and 2.6 (SD 2.9) for placebo (P = 0.216). Another trial reported mean Spielberger's Trait Anxiety Inventory scores of 47.56 (SD 11.68) for midazolam and 52.78 (SD 9.61) for placebo (P > 0.05). Intranasal Midazolam vs. Placebo (2 trials, 149 participants): Midazolam induced sedation (mean score: midazolam 3.15 [SD 0.36] vs. placebo 2.56 [SD 0.64]; P < 0.001) and reduced anxiety (mean score: midazolam 17.3 [SD 18.58] vs. placebo 49.3 [SD 29.46]; P < 0.001) in one trial with 54 participants. However, a meta-analysis of both trials found no significant difference in the risk of incomplete procedures (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.12; low-quality evidence). Conclusions: There is no high-quality evidence to definitively determine whether midazolam, when used as the sole sedative agent prior to procedures, is more or less effective than placebo or other medications. Low-quality evidence suggests that intravenous midazolam reduces anxiety compared to placebo. Evidence regarding oral midazolam's ability to reduce anxiety during procedures is inconsistent. Intranasal midazolam does not appear to reduce the risk of incomplete procedures, although it does provide sedation and anxiolysis. Moderate-quality evidence indicates that oral midazolam is less effective than chloral hydrate for completing procedures in children undergoing non-invasive diagnostic procedures.
